description:
Comportement surprenant de Quaks, le pélican blanc, qui suit les migrations de cigognes.

Le même individu a, semble-t-il, déjà été observé en 2008. Au lieu de suivre le parcours habituel passant par Israël pour rejoindre l'Afrique de l'Est, il a suivi une migration de cigogne jusqu'en Espagne où il passa l'hiver. Un parcours de plus de 1300 km traversant l'Allemagne, la Suisse, la France et l'Espagne.

Il est a noté qu'un individu a déjà été observé en 2002 sur l'étang du Lindre. Etait-ce déjà Quack ?

description: This observation documents a successful predation event by an adult Western Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis calurus) within the synanthropic micro-habitat of the Women Veterans Historic Rose Garden on the West Los Angeles VA Medical Center campus. The raptor, identified as an adult by its brick-red rectrices and dark patagial marks, utilized a "still-hunting" strategy from an elevated architectural perch on Building 220. Exploiting the "ecological trap" created by the garden’s star-shaped water feature, the hawk executed a vertical strike to capture a California Ground Squirrel (Otospermophilus beecheyi) that had ventured into the open hardscape to forage. Following the strike, the hawk exhibited immediate "mantling" behavior—posturing with spread wings to shield the kill from potential kleptoparasites like local corvids—before displacing to a nearby brick retaining wall to process the prey safely above ground level. description: A pair of Hawks circling overhead above a wooded hillside were spiraling up the slope. At least one of them was calling, making the familiar scream of a Red-Tail. Between those calls (three times in my slightly compressed recording above) were more prolonged plaintive whistles that I am not sure came from either of these birds. Perhaps they are those of a hungry fledgling following along? Or completely unrelated and coincidental? Strangely "Merlin" does not seem to respond to them, though they certainly sound birdlike. About those interspersed sounds I am puzzled. The two Hawks that I could see were 50-75 meters (165-245 feet) above the ground, moving away from a large lake in a mostly wooded County Park, toward more open cattle pastures to the southeast. The one of the two that I made a photo' of is an adult (sex unknowable?) I believe, with an unbanded tail.

description: Scarlet Macaw is one of the brightest, loudest, most magnificent natural wonder to be found in the Costa Rican rainforest. It’s truly a joy to observe them interacting with each other in their wild habitat. Scarlet Macaw (Ara macao) is on the CITES list: Appendix Level 1: "Species Threatened with Extinction." Trade in specimens of these species is permitted only in exceptional circumstances. CITES acromym stands for (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora). Macaws are critically endangered due to (mostly past) indiscriminate captures for the pet trade. In Costa Rica, it is illegal to own any kind of non-domestic animal, including parrots. Costa Rica sets a good example for having National rescue centers for birds. description: The cockatoos were raiding the orange tree in our yard like they do every orange season. It took a few big bites but lost the orange on the sloped roof and the two of them watched it roll off the roof and splat on the cement. They waited for a moment then went to pick another one. Its common for the cockatoos to start on a number of oranges and not finish a single one. description: Cassowary "W" with chicks "DD" and "EE" AUDIO The chicks engage in constant chatter: At the start of the recording there is a loud screech - the chick could no longer locate the adult male carer. Part way throught the recording there is a second slightly louder and different sound - this is one chick losing sight of the other chick. When the male adult carer heard the first loud screech he immediately and silently moved in the direction of the sound. He did not react to the second sound. The three constantly kept in touch, the chicks via sound, the adult via sight, never more than ten seconds from each other. When the recording was played back to them they all became extremely agitated. The adult male immediately showed agressive indications. Following this the adult male squatted down and the chicks hid under his body for a couple of minutes. Then they resumed chattter and looking for food. Guides hoping to gain status with recordings should note this. It is not good practice.

description: 5-6 magnificent Scarlet Macaws flying in for a landing onto Sea Almond trees. It was wonderful to see so many free flying scarlet macaws along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica. 30 years ago there were way fewer. We were told that keeping birds of any kind in a cage is illegal in Costa Rica, unless at a rehabilitation/rescue center. Some of the resorts along the coast have started putting up nesting boxes which the macaws are taking advantage of to reproduce :-) Scarlet Macaw (Ara macao) is a large red, yellow, and blue Central and South American parrot. It is native to humid evergreen forests of the Neotropics. It is about 81 cm (32 in) long, half is the pointed, graduated tail typical of all macaws. The scarlet macaw can live up to 75-90 years in captivity, although a more typical lifespan is 40 to 50 years. Scarlet macaws are often seen flying in pairs because they mate for life and fly together. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/19022-Ara-macao

Honestly I almost walked right past it because the camouflage was so good and it looked exactly like part of the cliff until it moved its head.

description: I’ve been copying and pasting the same paragraph to each observation in this batch, but I feel like this one deserves a little extra. Looking back at the past five months I think this was probably one of my favorite moments. I think it’s the most expressive that I’ve seen the owls. The baby leaning into Mom and then watching on as she prepares a meal was very sweet. Not to mention actually getting to watch the meal happen. What a privilege! Today was the first day in months that I’ve been unable to see any of the owl family when I went out to my local marsh. It seems as though the owlets have grown up faster than I expected, and are likely nearing the point where they can move on. I’m feeling a bit sad about that but also excited to share a lot of the photos that I’ve been taking. This batch of observations is from the past couple weeks and documents some of the last times I saw the owlets before they started branching🦉

description: El tucán grande (Ramphastos toco) es una especie de ave piciforme de la familia Ramphastidae, siendo su represetante de mayor tamaño y uno de los más conocidos. Tiene un plumaje llamativo con el cuerpo negro, garganta blanca y un anillo ocular azul. La característica más destacable es, como siempre, su enorme pico amarillo con una mancha negra, el cual pese a parecer pesado es increíblemente ligero dado que su interior es prácticamente hueco. Suelen tener una longitud media de 63 centímetros, de los cuales el pico ocupa unos 20cm y alcanzan un peso superior a 500 gramos. Tienen dos dedos hacia delante y dos hacia atrás, de forma que se pueden agarrar mejor a las ramas. No existe dimorfismo sexual entre machos y hembras. Esta especie se localiza en los bosques húmedos del Este de Sudamérica: Guayana, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brasil (Ecorregión del Cerrado) y el Noreste de Argentina . description: As I drove along a ranch road, a large shadow passed over me, and I assumed that it was just another Turkey Vulture or Red-tailed Hawk soaring overhead in northern Napa County. As I slowed down to stop, I saw a large brown bird with a very large wingspan gliding downwards towards a nearby hillside, and I quickly grabbed my camera. The Golden Eagle hit the ground with its legs outstretched like it was trying to catch something, but it was unsuccessful. After looking around for a few seconds, the Golden Eagle then began to "waddle-walk" about 30+ yards up the hillside instead of flying off, so I think that this is a juvenile bird, not yet very experienced in the "art" of hunting and flying, unless maybe it had some sort of injury. I have never seen an Eagle behave like this before. Private Property - No Public Access. Obsv #11,011

description: New Year's Day iNatting with Alice Herden (and her hubby) and Athena Phillips. We visited two spots today, one a lifer for me. 0800-1135: Perry Oldenburg Wildlife and Environmental Area -- We walked some of the perimeter, some of the powerline, and some of the nature trail. The weather at the start was clear and 52 degrees ("feels like" 52) with a light breeze. I photographed five Red-headed Woodpeckers. Pine Warblers were widespread and numerous; each record represents a different individual. Chipping Sparrows and American Goldfinches were also numerous along the southeastern fenceline; we found a Chipping Sparrow that was probably killed by an effing house cat. We left at 1136 and headed to Chinsegut Wildlife and Environmental Area, Big Pine Tract. 1150-1327: Chinsegut Wildlife and Environmental Area, Big Pine Tract -- A lifer spot for me, and I stayed behind to explore after the others had left. The weather at the start was sunny and 65 degrees ("feels like" 65) with a light breeze.

description: A friend of mine had set his backpack down on the beach while he went swimming in the ocean. Those of us still on the beach saw a huge baboon walking towards us (http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/1198219). We all took a few steps back, but the monkey went straight for the backpack and started rustling through its contents. One of my professors through his flip-flops at it, but the baboon did not leave. The baboon took off running down the beach, and the ostrich simply turned around and walked away.

description: With Valeri Ponzo; Day 3 of a three-day birding trip to southeastern Florida. Our itinerary for today was: 0706-0738: Everglades National Park, entrance station -- a successful chase of the Black-faced Grassquit. A Faithful Beauty moth was a great bonus (but my photograph of it is humorously bad!). The weather was post-rain: overcast, mild, and humid, with calm winds. Insects were not an issue. 0803-0808: SW 202nd Avenue at SW 256th Street, Homestead -- a quick stop for some Indian Peafowl. 0855-0856: SW 256th Street near SW 187th Avenue -- a Red-rumped Agouti (Dasyprocta leporina), a mammal that neither of us had heard of, ambled across the road in front us. I was able to take four photographs as it trotted away. Our record provides at least the eight for Florida, and the third for Miami-Dade County. Red-rumped Agouti is native to the West Indies and South America. https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/118698377 https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1001&contex

This incident evidences intention to perform extraordinary and difficult feats of aerobatics just for the fun of it among bald eagles. description: Südlicher Scharlachara, Hellroter Ara oder Arakanga (Ara macao macao) - Guacamayo rojo sudamericano. [Die Tiere in der Golfo-Dulce-Region haben gelernt, sich von den Früchten des Seemandelbaumes (Terminalia catappa) zu ernähren, der hier mittlerweile als heimisch gilt, aber ursprünglich aus dem australpazifischen Raum stammt. Sie knacken dazu die mandelartigen Früchte mit ihren scharfen Schnäbeln. Die Spezies wird auch Gelbflügelara genannt, um sie vom südamerikanischen Grünflügelara oder Dunkelroten Ara (Ara chloropterus) zu unterscheiden.] The South American Scarlet macaws in the Golfo Dulce region have adapted to feeding on the fruit of the Indian almond tree (Terminalia catappa), which is now considered native to the area but originally comes from the Austral-Pacific region. They crack open the almond-like fruit with their sharp beaks to access the core. This species is also called Red-and-yellow macaw to distinguish it from the South American Green-winged Macaw (Ara chloropterus).

One hopped out and stood on the fence for about 20 seconds. The others popped in and out of view in the hedge. I had been standing a few metres away for a few minutes beforehand checking on our new native bee hive. When the one on the fence hopped out I thought it would be startled that I was there but it didn't seem too concerned. description: Wild cassowary with young one (this obs). Wandered onto the road and bus stopped and waited respectfully for 5 minutes whilst it stood in front of the bus (I am sure the passengers were enjoying the sight). Then it slowly mooched off the road and hung around the road edge with its little one for a few minutes. Gradually wandered down into the bush. I was behind the bus and pulled over and stood on the road edge with my camera. The mother seemed in a calm mood and showed no signs of being bothered by the vehicles or couple of us standing on th roadside. We stood dead still and enjoyed the encounter. The mother stayed within about 10-15 metres of both the young one and us. At one point the curious young one came right up close to us, so we backed off a bit. Then it lost interest and went to find its mum in the bush nearby below the road. A great experience.
